questions.q: According to this lesson, what three qualities does a development environment most need to support?
options: Maximum data volume, long refresh cycles, and broad user access
Speed, low cost, and isolation between different builders' in-progress work
Full production data, 24/7 uptime guarantees, and a dedicated support contract
Read-only access for every user in the org
questions.explain: Development environments need to be fast to create and reset, cheap enough to run several at once, and isolated so one developer's unfinished work doesn't collide with another's.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a sandbox and a scratch org as development-tier tools?
options: A scratch org is a long-lived, persistent copy of an org's metadata, while a sandbox is temporary and built from a definition file
Sandboxes and scratch orgs are two names for the exact same feature
Scratch orgs can only be created by Salesforce Support, not by developers
A sandbox is a long-lived copy of an org's metadata that persists until refreshed or deleted, while a scratch org is temporary, disposable, and built from a source-driven definition file
questions.explain: A sandbox persists as a copy of the org until someone refreshes or deletes it; a scratch org is disposable by design and recreated from a definition file rather than copied.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say isolation, not data realism, is the core design problem at the development tier?
options: Because the main risk at this stage is two builders' changes colliding in a shared environment, not whether the data looks like production
Because development environments never need any configuration at all
Because Salesforce technically prevents more than one developer from ever using the same sandbox
Because data realism only matters in production, never in any non-production environment
questions.explain: At the development tier, a half-built change from one developer landing in the same environment another developer is actively testing is the main failure mode -- which is an isolation problem, not a data-realism problem.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes a scratch org safe to delete and recreate without losing work, in a source-driven development approach?
options: Scratch orgs automatically back themselves up to a hidden production copy
Scratch orgs cannot actually be deleted once created
Every change of real value is committed to version control, so the scratch org itself holds nothing that doesn't also exist in source
Salesforce support manually recovers deleted scratch orgs on request
questions.explain: In source-driven development, the scratch org's true state lives in version control -- nothing of real value exists only inside the disposable org itself, which is exactly what makes throwing it away safe.

questions.q: Four developers share one Developer sandbox, and two report that Flows they were testing kept breaking without them changing anything. What does this lesson identify as the likely root cause?
options: A Salesforce platform outage affecting only Flows
The sandbox had expired and needed to be recreated from a definition file
Flows are not supported in Developer sandboxes at all
Multiple developers building and testing simultaneously in the same shared environment, where one person's in-progress changes collide with another's
questions.explain: This is the classic symptom of insufficient isolation at the development tier -- a shared environment lets one person's unfinished work break what someone else is actively testing, which is why the standard fix is giving each builder their own environment.
